finding_info.title: Ensure that root is the only user with UID 0
finding_info.desc: Multiple accounts with UID 0 are root-equivalent for filesystem and process semantics. An attacker who creates one bypasses every name-based audit and detection that watches the literal `root` user.

remediation.desc: Identify the offending account in `/etc/passwd` and either delete it or assign it a fresh non-zero UID. Investigate how it was created.

finding_info.title: Ensure no duplicate user names exist
finding_info.desc: Duplicate user names indicate hand-edited passwd or merged user databases. Tools may resolve only the first match, masking permissions and audit attribution on the shadowed entry.

remediation.desc: Edit `/etc/passwd` to remove or rename the duplicate. Investigate the source.

finding_info.title: Ensure no duplicate UIDs exist
finding_info.desc: Two user names sharing one UID makes ownership and audit logs ambiguous: a file owned by UID X cannot be reliably attributed to one principal, undermining accountability and forensics.

remediation.desc: Renumber duplicates via `usermod -u <new-uid> <name>` and `chown -R` their files. Investigate the duplicate's origin.

finding_info.title: Ensure that `/etc/securetty` is empty
finding_info.desc: An empty (or missing) `/etc/securetty` disables direct root login on every console, physical and virtual, forcing administrators to log in as themselves and sudo to root, which preserves audit attribution.

remediation.desc: Truncate the file or remove it.

finding_info.title: Ensure no login is available on system accounts
finding_info.desc: System accounts (UID < 1000) own daemons, not humans, granting them an interactive shell turns each one into a possible login target.

remediation.desc: For each offending system account: `usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin <name>`.

finding_info.title: Ensure all passwords are hashed with yescrypt
finding_info.desc: Hashes from older algorithms (DES, MD5, SHA-256/512 crypt) are far cheaper to crack on modern GPUs than yescrypt (which also requires RAM to crack/calculate).

remediation.desc: Edit PAM passwd to use yescrypt when changing password, and force users to change passwords `passwd --expire <user>`.

finding_info.title: Ensure no user account is expired, delete them
finding_info.desc: User accounts (UID >= 1000) past their expiration date are disabled but still clutter the user database and risk being re-enabled accidentally. If an account is no longer needed, deletion is cleaner than indefinite expiration. System accounts are ignored, expiration is a common way to park them.

remediation.desc: After confirming the account is not needed: `userdel -r <name>`. Investigate any expired account whose home dir still contains active data before deleting.

finding_info.title: Ensure that all home directories exist
finding_info.desc: A missing home directory referenced from `/etc/passwd` could be created by an attacker, and could include configurations that could lead to privilege escalation or persistence.

remediation.desc: Either re-create the missing directory with the right ownership and 0700 permissions, or remove the user with `userdel`.

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/shadow` password fields are not empty
finding_info.desc: An empty password field in `/etc/shadow` lets that account log in with no password at all, on any service that consults shadow (login, ssh PasswordAuthentication, etc.).

remediation.desc: Lock the account immediately: `passwd -l <name>`; then either set a real password `passwd <name>` or delete the account.

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/passwd` password fields are not empty
finding_info.desc: An empty password field, instead of `x` in `/etc/passwd`, means the system reads the password directly from passwd and treats absence as no password required.

remediation.desc: Run `pwconv` to migrate password fields to `/etc/shadow`, investigate any user with an empty field.

finding_info.title: Ensure accounts in `/etc/passwd` use shadowed passwords
finding_info.desc: Password hashes in `/etc/passwd` are world-readable, exposing every account's hash to any local user for cracking.

remediation.desc: Run `pwconv` to migrate hashes to `/etc/shadow`, verify all password fields in `/etc/passwd` are `x`.

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/passwd` file permissions are `644`
finding_info.desc: Looser permissions on `/etc/passwd` let unprivileged users edit account metadata (UID, shell, home dir) and grant themselves access, tighter than 0644 breaks userland tools that need to resolve user names.

remediation.desc: `chmod 644 /etc/passwd`

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/passwd` file owner is `root:root` or file is missing
finding_info.desc: If `/etc/passwd` is owned by a non-root user, that user can edit account UIDs and shells, granting themselves UID 0 or pointing root's shell at malicious code.

remediation.desc: `chown root:root /etc/passwd`

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/shadow` file owner is correct
finding_info.desc: Wrong ownership on `/etc/shadow` lets a non-root principal read every account's password hash for offline cracking, or rewrite hashes to take over arbitrary accounts.

remediation.desc:
On Debian: `chown root:shadow /etc/shadow`
On other distros: `chown root:root /etc/shadow`

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/shadow` file permissions are correct
finding_info.desc: Loose permissions on `/etc/shadow` expose every account's password hash to non-root users, who can then crack them.

remediation.desc:
On Debian: `chmod 640 /etc/shadow`
On other distros: `chmod 600 /etc/shadow`

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/shadow-` file owner is correct or file is missing
finding_info.desc: `/etc/shadow-` is the previous-generation backup of shadow, if its ownership is wrong, an attacker can recover password hashes from the backup that the live file's tighter ownership would have blocked.

remediation.desc:
On Debian: `chown root:shadow /etc/shadow-`
On other distros: `chown root:root /etc/shadow-`

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/shadow-` file permissions are correct or file is missing
finding_info.desc: Loose permissions on the shadow backup file leak the same password hashes as the live file.

remediation.desc:
On Debian: `chmod 640 /etc/shadow-`
On other distros: `chmod 600 /etc/shadow-`

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/security/opasswd` file owner is `root:root` or file is missing
finding_info.desc: `/etc/security/opasswd` stores previously-used password hashes for `pam_pwhistory` reuse prevention. Wrong ownership exposes those historical hashes to non-root users for cracking, leaking old password that could indicate patterns or be reused elsewhere.

remediation.desc: `chown root:root /etc/security/opasswd`

finding_info.title: Ensure `/etc/security/opasswd` file permissions are `600` or file is missing
finding_info.desc: `/etc/security/opasswd` stores previously-used password hashes for `pam_pwhistory` reuse prevention. Wrong permissions exposes those historical hashes to non-root users for cracking, leaking old password that could indicate patterns or be reused elsewhere.

remediation.desc: `chmod 600 /etc/security/opasswd`

finding_info.title: Ensure no users have `.rhosts` or `.shosts` files
finding_info.desc: Legacy .rhosts files enable trust-based authentication without passwords, a major security risk. If an attacker compromises any trusted host, they can log in as any user on this system without credentials.

remediation.desc: Remove all .rhosts, .shosts files from user home directories: `find /home -name '.rhosts' -delete`

finding_info.title: Ensure all users' home directories are owned by their respective user
finding_info.desc: Home directories owned by other users could allow unauthorized access to files. An attacker could read private keys, configuration files, or plant malicious files.

remediation.desc: `chown <username>:<username> /home/<username>`

finding_info.title: Ensure all users' home directories have permissions 750 or stricter
finding_info.desc: World-writable or world-readable home directories expose private user data to other users on the system. Permissions should be 750 or stricter to prevent unauthorized access.

remediation.desc: `chmod 750 /home/<username>`

finding_info.title: Ensure no users have world-writable files in their home directory
finding_info.desc: World-writable files in user home directories can be modified by any user on the system, enabling data tampering and potential privilege escalation via .bashrc, .profile, or crontab modification.

remediation.desc: Find and fix: `find /home -type f -perm -0002 -exec chmod o-w {} \;`

finding_info.title: Ensure root account is disabled
finding_info.desc: An enabled root account with a valid password and an interactive shell is the single highest-value target for brute-force and credential-theft attacks. Disabling it forces administrators to log in as themselves and use `sudo`, which preserves non-repudiable audit trails. Ensure you have valid admin accounts.

remediation.desc: Lock the password: `passwd -l root` and set the shell to nologin: `usermod -s /usr/sbin/nologin root`.

finding_info.title: Ensure account is disabled when password is expired
finding_info.desc: Set the number of days after a password expires until the account is permanently disabled to instantly. Password expiry could mean that the account should rotate it's password, or that the password was compromised, in either case the account should be locked to prevent it from being used until the password is changed. Only user accounts (UID >= 1000) are checked, system accounts don't login with a password. Especially useful when doing mandatory password rotation, but be careful to always keep a valid access to the host.

findings.message: audit, dupuser, dupuser, ghost, nopass, expired

remediation.desc: Set a user inactivity_period to 0: `chage -I 0 <username>`.

finding_info.title: Ensure account is disabled when password is expired by default
finding_info.desc: Set the number of days after a password expires until the account is permanently disabled to instantly. Password expiry could mean that the account should rotate it's password, or that the password was compromised, in either case the account should be locked to prevent it from being used until the password is changed. Especially useful when doing mandatory password rotation, but be careful to always keep a valid access to the host.

remediation.desc: Edit useradd configuration in: `/etc/default/useradd` and set: `INACTIVE=0`.
